title: Why enums are not generic, and what to use instead

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: Per this page, why does `enum Setting<T> { MAX_RETRIES(3), APP_NAME("MyApp"); }` fail to compile in Java 21?

options.text: Erasure removes the per-constant type arguments before the program runs
options.says: The page says the rule is not a consequence of erasure: a generic class can already declare static final instances with different type arguments.

options.text: The feature exists but stays behind the preview flag until a later release
options.says: The page says JEP 301, which proposed generic enums, was withdrawn, so there is no preview to enable.

options.text: The language forbids type parameters on an enum, and JEP 301 was withdrawn
options.says: The page calls it a language-design decision: the enum declaration takes no type parameters, and JEP 301, which proposed them, was withdrawn.

questions.stem: Per this page, which workaround checks the type of each value only at run time?

options.text: Constants of one enum type, each holding a Class object
options.says: The page describes the Class-token enum as storing a Class<?> in each constant for runtime type checking, with no compile-time guarantee.

options.text: Records permitted by one sealed interface, one per value
options.says: The page presents the sealed-interface pattern as the one with full compile-time type safety.

options.text: Static final instances of one generic class, one per value
options.says: The page says static final instances give full generic typing, so their types are checked by the compiler.

concepts: An enum declaration cannot take type parameters; this is a language-design decision rather than erasure, and JEP 301, which proposed generic enums, was withdrawn.
Each workaround trades something: the Class-token enum keeps EnumSet and switch but checks only at run time, while sealed records and static instances type fully but lose EnumSet and EnumMap.
